# About RML and Associates CPAs LLC

## Identity

RML and Associates CPAs LLC is a CPA firm based in Laramie, Wyoming. It provides accounting and bookkeeping, tax preparation, and advisory services. Its tagline is "Accounting, tax, and advisory is what we do best." The firm serves clients across Wyoming, Nebraska and Colorado, and describes itself as an experienced team that serves clients with integrity, honesty and excellent work.

**Core values:** professionalism, responsiveness and quality.

**Team**
- **Megan Hanneman, CGMA**, Shareholder.
- **Liz Powers, CPA**, Shareholder. Her technology expertise is recognized by the AICPA. She is also the firm's primary contact.
- **Sherrie McKinney**, Accounting Services.

**Core services**
- **Business tax:** state and federal income tax preparation and filing, local and state sales tax compliance, state and federal payroll tax, profit and loss statements, mergers and acquisitions, and entity selection and structure (S-Corp, C-Corp, LLC). Year-round planning and deadline management are part of the service.
- **Personal income tax:** accurate, on-time returns, tax planning strategies, electronic filing and direct deposit, and filing extensions and estimated tax calculations.
- **Payroll:** the firm helps clients get set up on payroll.

**Voice and tone:** friendly, reassuring and professional, with a local, personal emphasis on integrity and responsiveness. The firm aims to sound warm, positive and helpful. Brand adjectives: approachable, professional, trustworthy, local, personal. Example of the firm's voice: "We're glad to help you look ahead so you can plan with confidence. Have a question about your taxes? Call us. We'll take the time to walk you through it and make sure it makes sense."

**Contact**
- 505 S. 3rd Street, Suite 100, Laramie, WY 82070
- Phone: (307) 755-1040
- Fax: (307) 742-4944
- Email: info@rmlcpas.com
- Website: https://rmlcpas.com
- Hours: Monday to Friday, 8 AM to 12 PM and 1 to 5 PM. Closed Saturday and Sunday.

## Positioning & Differentiation

**Positioning statement:** Laramie's CPA firm, serving clients across Wyoming, Nebraska and Colorado with accounting, tax and advisory services tailored to each client. We look ahead so you can plan with confidence. The firm specializes in agriculture, restaurants, retail, professional practices, real estate and non-profits.

**What sets the firm apart**
- **Locally owned and independent.** Services can be tailored to each client's needs.
- **BDO Alliance USA.** The firm is an independent member.
- **Credentialed leadership.** Megan Hanneman holds the CGMA designation. Liz Powers is a CPA with AICPA-recognized technology expertise.
- **Explanation, not just compliance.** The firm takes the time to walk clients through their taxes and financial statements so the numbers make sense.
- **Responsiveness.** Responsiveness is one of the firm's stated core values, and clients are invited to call with questions.
- **Free consultation.** The firm offers a free consultation.

**Client feedback:** A non-profit client said: "The entire RML team had been incredible to work with for all my nonprofit accounting needs. They really care about making it as simple as possible for everyone to understand accounting & communicate so quickly. I'm grateful for the support RML has given my organization."

**Content emphasis:** tax planning (business and personal), new business formation, succession planning, estate planning and trust tax services, agriculture (farming, ranching, drought deferrals), restaurant tip credits, and real estate agents, brokers and portfolio investors.

## Industries Served

The firm's ideal clients are agriculture and ranching operations, restaurants, retail businesses, professional services firms and practices, real estate businesses and investors, and non-profit organizations, associations, foundations and charities. The two industries below have dedicated focus areas.

### Non-Profit Organizations

**Who:** Associations, foundations, charities and other service organizations.

**Value proposition**
- **Compliance without the stress.** The firm prepares Form 990 and 990-T and keeps clients compliant with state law, so tax-exempt status is never at risk.
- **Financials your board can understand.** The firm walks board and staff through the financial statements and explains what the numbers mean.
- **Audit-ready and funder-ready.** Annual audits and reviewed or compiled statements are prepared to meet the requirements of funders and the state.

**Pain points**
- Form 990 and 990-T filing is complex, and errors or late filings risk tax-exempt status.
- Board members and funders expect clear, timely financial statements, but staff often lack accounting expertise.
- Grant and restricted-fund accounting is hard to track and report.
- Audit, review or compilation requirements vary by funder and state.
- State law compliance and registration deadlines are easy to miss with small or volunteer-run teams.
- Limited budgets make full-time finance staff hard to justify.
- 501(c)(3) setup and Form 1023 are intimidating for new organizations.

**Services:** annual audits, quarterly and annual financial statements, reviewed or compiled statements, Forms 990 and 990-T, supporting schedules, state law compliance, and 501(c)(3) applications including Form 1023. Form 990 preparation and exempt-organization compliance is a confirmed focus area.

**Typical triggers:** a funder requires an audit, a filing is missed or late, the board turns over, or a bookkeeper or finance staff member leaves.

### Real Estate

**Who:** Real estate businesses and investors, including agents, brokers, portfolio investors and flippers.

**Value proposition**
- **Tax planning before the deal.** The firm models the tax impact of buying, flipping, holding or exchanging a property before the client commits, so there are no surprises at closing.
- **Real estate-specific tax strategy.** This covers depreciation, 1031 exchanges, entity structure and deductions for agents, brokers and investors.
- **Clean books by property.** Property-level bookkeeping and financial reports satisfy lenders and partners.

**Pain points: agents and brokers**
- Irregular commission-based 1099 income makes estimated taxes hard to plan.
- Business expenses such as mileage, marketing, licensing and home office are poorly tracked and under-deducted.
- They are unsure whether an S-corp or LLC structure would save money.
- Business and personal finances are not separated, so books are messy.
- Cash flow swings with market and closing timelines.

**Pain points: portfolio investors and flippers**
- Buy, flip and hold strategies are taxed differently (capital gains vs. ordinary income, dealer status).
- Depreciation, cost segregation and passive loss rules are confusing.
- 1031 exchange timing and rules are strict and costly to get wrong.
- Property-level books are hard to keep separate across properties and entities.
- Entity structure and liability protection get messy as a portfolio grows.
- Lenders and partners want clean property-level financials.
- Tax liability is hard to forecast around sales.

**Typical triggers**
- A big sale or flip closes and brings an unexpected tax bill.
- A second or third property is purchased, or the portfolio outgrows current bookkeeping.
- An agent's or broker's income jumps, or they move from W-2 to 1099 and want to know if an S-corp or LLC would help.
- A 1031 exchange or property sale is coming and they need guidance on timing.
- Their current preparer misses deductions or depreciation, or doesn't respond.
- A lender or partner asks for clean property-level financials.

### Personal income tax
URL: /personal-income-tax

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: tax-return-review.jpg | alt: "CPA reviewing a personal tax return with a client at a desk" | query: "accountant reviewing tax return with client" -->
## Personal income tax preparation in Laramie, WY: accurate and filed on time

Personal income tax preparation in Laramie, WY comes down to two things: the return is right, and it's filed by the deadline. A CPA prepares your return, checks it against your income forms and last year's filing, and walks you through anything that looks different this time.

Federal and state tax return filing is handled start to finish. Your return is filed electronically, and if you're owed a refund, direct deposit gets it to your bank account faster than a paper check. If you owe, you'll know the amount and the due date before you file, not after.

Need more time? Filing extensions and estimated tax calculations are part of the service, so a busy month doesn't leave you scrambling. Have a W-2, a stack of 1099s, or both? Bring them. The goal is a return that makes sense to you, too.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Do I still need to file in another state if Wyoming has no income tax?

Wyoming doesn't tax personal income at the state level, which leads some people to assume filing is simple. Sometimes it is. But income doesn't always stay inside the state line.

Work a season in Colorado, own a rental in Nebraska, or run an operation that crosses a border, and another state may expect a return from you. RML serves clients across Wyoming, Nebraska and Colorado, so these questions come up all the time.

Tax return preparation for individuals in Albany County, WY often starts with one plain question: where did your income come from? Answer that, and we'll tell you which returns you need to file. Rules vary by state and by situation, so ask before you assume.

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col -->
## Returns for self-employed, commission, ranch, and restaurant owners

Self-employed personal tax filing in Laramie looks different from a single W-2 return. Income arrives unevenly, expenses cross between business and personal, and the numbers need a CPA's eye.

### Real estate agents, brokers and portfolio investors
icon: Home

Commission checks arrive on no schedule, and 1099 income makes estimated taxes hard to predict. We help you set payments that fit what you actually earn, and we track mileage and other business expenses so they reach your return. ### Farm and ranch owners

Ranch income swings with weather and markets. Returns for farm and ranch owners include drought-related deferrals, handled with a clear record of why and when. See how we work with [agriculture clients](/industries/agriculture).

### Restaurant owners
icon: Receipt

Tip credits earned by the restaurant flow through to the owner's personal return. We review the business figures alongside your personal filing so the two agree. Learn more about our [restaurant clients](/industries/restaurants).

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: year-round-planning.jpg | alt: "Calendar and calculator on a desk beside a planning notebook" | query: "tax planning calendar calculator desk" -->
## How can I plan ahead so tax season holds no surprises?

We look ahead so you can plan with confidence. For your personal return, that means a conversation before the year ends, not a bill in April.

Planning strategies are built around your real numbers: your income, your deductions, your goals. Estimated tax calculations keep quarterly payments close to what you will owe. If you need more time, a filing extension is on the table.

The moments that cause the most trouble are big ones. A sale closes. You buy a second property. A flip pays off sooner than expected. Each can create a tax bill nobody saw coming.

Call us while the deal is still open. We'll talk through how the deal may affect your return, so you can decide with the full picture. We won't promise a savings number, because honest planning starts with your facts.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: laramie-cpa-office.jpg | alt: "Local CPA greeting a client in a bright Laramie office" | query: "friendly accountant greeting client office" -->

A big-box tax counter or a seasonal storefront can file your return. What they can't always do is pick up the phone in July when you have a question about an estimated payment.

RML is locally owned. The same team is here year-round, and we're an independent member of the BDO Alliance USA. Our core values are professionalism, responsiveness and quality, and they show up in small ways: a call returned, a question answered in plain English, a return walked through with you.

Because the firm is self-owned, service fits each client rather than a script. A first-time filer and a rancher with several income sources get different conversations.

Looking for affordable tax return prep in Laramie? Start with the free consultation. You'll hear what the work involves and what to expect before you commit to anything.

## Laramie accounting built around how you operate

RML and Associates CPAs LLC is a locally owned, self-owned CPA firm in Laramie that provides accounting services in Laramie, WY and across Wyoming, Nebraska and Colorado. Nobody above us hands down a template, so your accounting is set up around how your operation really runs.

We work with [agriculture and ranching operations](/industries/agriculture), [restaurants](/industries/restaurants), [retail shops](/industries/retail), [professional practices](/industries/professional-services), [real estate agents and investors](/industries/real-estate), and [non-profits](/industries/nonprofits) across Wyoming, Nebraska and Colorado. As a CPA firm in Laramie, Wyoming, our job is simple: keep your numbers current so you can look ahead and plan with confidence. Not sure what you need? Start with a free consultation. We'll listen first, then tell you plainly what we would do.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: monthly-bookkeeping-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing monthly bookkeeping reports with a business owner at a desk" | query: "accountant reviewing bookkeeping reports with client" -->
## Monthly bookkeeping that is ready before you ask

Every month we reconcile your accounts, categorize your transactions and prepare a profit and loss statement. Because the books stay clean all year, your business tax preparation starts from finished numbers instead of a scramble in March. It is outsourced accounting for owners who would rather run the business than chase the ledger, and it works with QuickBooks or the platform you already use.

The details change by operation. For ranchers, we keep records that support drought deferral decisions, so a forced livestock sale is documented properly when dry conditions hit. For restaurant owners, we track tip credits as they happen, so the paperwork is ready when the return is. Retail and professional services owners get something simpler and just as valuable: a clear answer to what the month actually earned.

Monthly bookkeeping in Laramie should not feel like a mystery. When a number looks off, we call you, explain it and fix it.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: payroll-setup-meeting.jpg | alt: "Business owner and accountant setting up payroll together on a laptop" | query: "accountant helping owner set up payroll laptop" -->
## How do I get my team set up on payroll?

Starting payroll, or changing how you run it, is where small mistakes turn into big notices. If you are looking for payroll services in Laramie, WY, we help you get set up the right way: we walk you through the setup, confirm your pay schedule and withholding, and connect payroll to your books so wages post correctly from the first pay period. 

Because state and federal payroll tax is already part of our [Business Tax](/business-tax) work, your deposits and filings stay accurate and on time. If a payroll question comes up later, call us and we will walk through it with you.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: cloud-accounting-migration.jpg | alt: "Accountant showing an owner online accounting software on a laptop screen" | query: "accountant cloud accounting software laptop client" -->
## How do I move from desktop software to cloud accounting?

Still running QuickBooks Desktop and wondering if it is time to move online? It may be, and the switch does not have to be stressful. Liz Powers, CPA, guides our cloud-accounting work. We look at how your current file is set up, clean up old accounts, duplicates and uncleared items, then move your data to an online system. Before you go live, we check that your opening balances match, so your reports still tie out. You keep your history, your books stay accurate through the change, and we explain each step in plain language.

## Find the right form in under a minute

You're in the right place. This page gathers the forms, documents and helpful links our clients ask for most, sorted by the kind of work you do. RML and Associates CPAs is based in Laramie and serves clients across Wyoming, Nebraska and Colorado, so wherever you file from, start here.

Pick the category that fits you:

## Advisory for farms and ranches, from drought deferrals to succession

- Who takes over management, and who simply owns a share.

- How to treat heirs who are not involved in the day-to-day work.

## Resources

### How to turn a second home into a tax win
URL: /resources/how-to-turn-a-second-home-into-a-tax-win

Most second home owners in Laramie pick the place for the view, then find out later that the IRS cares a great deal about how many nights they actually slept there. A cabin in the Snowy Range, a condo in Fort Collins or a lake place in Colorado can be a quiet tax shelter or a rental business with its own paperwork. The difference comes down to a day count, and you control it.

This post walks through the second home tax rules that matter most, with a worked example in dollars. It also covers a few wrinkles that come up for people who work and volunteer in Laramie's nonprofit community: board members, executive directors, development staff and the organizations they serve.

## Three buckets decide how the IRS treats your second home

The IRS sorts every second home into one of three buckets based on two numbers: days you rent it at a fair price, and days you use it personally. The details are in [IRS Publication 527](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p527), and the short version looks like this.

| Your year | How the IRS treats it | What it means on your return |
|---|---|---|
| Rented fewer than 15 days | Personal residence | Rent is tax-free and not reported. Rental expenses are not deductible. |
| Rented 15 or more days, and personal use is more than the greater of 14 days or 10% of rental days | Residence with rental use | Rent is reported. Expenses are deductible only up to the rental income, so no loss. |
| Rented 15 or more days, and personal use is no more than the greater of 14 days or 10% of rental days | Rental property | Full rental deductions, including depreciation. A loss is possible, subject to passive loss limits. |

That first row is the part people like. If you rent the place for 14 days or fewer, the income is tax-free. A Laramie house rented for a handful of days around a Wyoming Cowboys home game or commencement weekend can bring in real money that never shows up on your return. This is the IRS 14-day rule for a second home, and it is one of the few places the tax code simply hands you a break.

The second and third rows are where owners get surprised. Crossing from one to the other can change your return by thousands of dollars.

## Which days count as personal use

Personal use is broader than "the nights I slept there." Under Publication 527, a day counts as personal use when:

- You or a family member use the home, even if the relative pays rent at a below-market rate.
- Someone uses it under a swap or reciprocal arrangement, like trading weeks with a friend's property.
- Anyone uses it while paying less than a fair rental price.

Days you spend there mostly doing repairs and maintenance generally do not count as personal use. A weekend of scraping and restaining the deck is a work weekend, as long as you actually work most of the day. Keep a log that says so.

Because fair rental price is the test, your brother paying you half of market rate for a week turns that week into a personal week. Rental days stay rental days only when the rent is real.

## A Snowy Range cabin, worked in dollars

Here is a realistic example. A Laramie couple owns a cabin in the Snowy Range. They rent it for 60 nights at an average of $200, so rental income is $12,000. Their yearly costs look like this:

- Mortgage interest: $8,000
- Property taxes: $2,400
- Utilities, insurance, cleaning and repairs: $6,000
- Depreciation, if the home qualifies as rental property: $9,000

**Scenario A: 14 personal days.** The couple stays 14 nights. That is not more than the greater of 14 days or 10% of 60 rental days (6 days), so the cabin is rental property. Total use is 74 days, so the rental share is 60 divided by 74, or about 81%. Deductible rental expenses come to roughly $20,600 against $12,000 of income. That is a paper loss of about $8,600.

Whether the loss helps now depends on the passive loss rules. If you actively participate in the rental and your modified adjusted gross income is $100,000 or less, you can generally deduct up to $25,000 of rental loss against other income. That allowance shrinks by 50 cents for every dollar of income over $100,000 and disappears at $150,000. A couple earning $120,000 could use the full $8,600 now. A couple at $160,000 would carry it forward to future years.

**Scenario B: 20 personal days.** Six more nights at the cabin pushes personal use past 14 days, so the cabin becomes a residence with rental use. Total use is 80 days and the rental share drops to 75%. Their share of interest and property taxes is $7,800, and operating costs are limited to what the $12,000 of income can absorb, about $4,200. Depreciation is zero. Net rental income is zero, and there is no loss.

Six extra nights cost this couple an $8,600 deduction. Nothing about the cabin changed. That is why we like to talk before the year starts rather than in March.

## Mortgage interest and property taxes still work in your favor

Even when the home is classed as a residence, you generally keep your mortgage interest and property tax deductions if you itemize. Interest on a second home is generally deductible on loans up to $750,000 in total acquisition debt across your main and second homes for loans taken out after December 15, 2017. The federal cap on state and local tax deductions still applies to property taxes.

On a rented vacation home, the share of interest and taxes that is not allocated to rental use moves to your personal itemized deductions. Nothing is wasted, but the deduction lands on a different part of the return, and whether it helps depends on whether you itemize at all. Many Laramie households take the standard deduction, so an itemized interest deduction may be worth less than it sounds.

## Nonprofit wrinkles that most second home articles skip

People in Laramie's nonprofit world use their personal property for the cause more often than they realize. A few situations are worth a second look.

**Donating a week at your cabin to a gala auction.** This is generous and popular. But Publication 527 treats it as personal use if the charity sells the stay and someone uses it. You also generally cannot deduct the value of donated use of your property. One donated week can push you over the 14-day line in the table above, so count it.

**Hosting a board retreat or staff planning weekend.** If the organization pays a fair rental price, those are rental days, and you report the income. If it pays little or nothing, those are personal days for you. Either way, write down the dates and the rate. A rental at an inflated price is also a problem, since the IRS and the organization's own conflict-of-interest policy will both want to see how the price was set.

**Receiving a donated vacation home.** If your organization is given a cabin or condo and then rents it out, rent from real property is generally excluded from unrelated business income. Debt on the property can change that. When there is a mortgage, the debt-financed rules may require a Form 990-T. We check this early, because a gift that creates an unexpected filing is easier to fix before the first rental season. Our [nonprofit accounting work](/industries/nonprofits) includes Form 990 and 990-T preparation, so these questions are routine for us.

**Buying with a salary that fluctuates.** Nonprofit compensation can be steady, but grant cycles, bonuses and spouse income can push you above or below the $100,000 to $150,000 passive loss phase-out range from year to year. Where you land in that range affects how useful a rental loss is, so the same cabin can be worth more in one year than in the next.

## Decide before you buy, not after the first rental

The question to answer is how you intend to use the place. Three plans, three different results:

- **Mostly personal, with a few rented days.** Keep rentals to 14 days or fewer and the income is tax-free. You give up rental deductions, and that is fine, since there is no income to offset.
- **Mixed use.** Rent it often enough to cover costs, and use it more than 14 days. Expect the income to be roughly offset by expenses, with no loss to claim.
- **Rental first.** Rent it most of the year and keep personal use at or under 14 days (or 10% of rental days, if that is higher). You get depreciation and potential losses, and also bookkeeping duties, sales and lodging tax filings, and a passive loss calculation each year.

A second home bought as an investment property follows the same rules as any other rental, and that is where [a CPA who works with real estate owners](/industries/real-estate) earns their fee. We can model the tax impact of each plan before you sign, using your actual income, loan terms and rental estimates. That includes the break-even number of rental nights.

## Records that make the numbers hold up

A calendar is the most useful document you can keep. Mark every night as rental, personal or maintenance, and note the rate for anything that is not a standard booking. Keep your closing statement, loan statements, property tax bills, cleaning invoices and any platform payout reports. If you rent for more than a few days, a separate bank account for the property keeps your personal and rental money apart.

The IRS also publishes a plain-language summary in [Tax Topic 415](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc415) if you want a second source. Your [personal return](/personal-income-tax) is where all of this lands, so the calendar matters more than any software.

## Common Questions

**What is the IRS 14-day rule for a second home?**

If you rent your home for fewer than 15 days in a year, the rental income is tax-free and you do not report it. You also cannot deduct rental expenses. A separate 14-day test compares your personal use to rental days to decide whether the home counts as a residence or as rental property.

**Can I deduct a loss on a second home I rent out?**

Only if the home counts as rental property, meaning personal use is no more than the greater of 14 days or 10% of rental days. Even then, passive loss rules apply. With active participation and income under $100,000, up to $25,000 may be deductible, phasing out completely at $150,000.

**Does a nonprofit board retreat at my cabin count as personal use?**

It does if the organization pays you less than a fair rental price, or nothing. If it pays the market rate, it counts as a rental day. Either way, document the dates and the rate, and check your nonprofit's conflict-of-interest policy before accepting payment.

## Talk it through before the next rental season

If you are weighing a second home purchase, or you already own one and want to know where the day count puts you, call RML and Associates CPAs LLC. We are a locally owned Laramie firm, and we will walk through your calendar, your loan and your income, then tell you which bucket fits and what each plan costs in taxes. Your first consultation is free, and you can [contact us here](/contact) to set a time.

### Do the math behind renting vs. buying a home
URL: /resources/do-the-math-behind-renting-vs-buying-a-home

The conversation usually starts with two numbers: what you pay in rent now and what a mortgage "would be." Neither is the whole comparison. If you work for a Laramie nonprofit, serve on its board, or run it, the decision also touches grant-cycle job security, a salary that may not grow fast, and a down payment that is probably most of your savings.

This post walks through the math the way we would at a coffee meeting. It uses illustrative numbers, so swap in your own.

## Start with your personal financial statement

A personal financial statement is a one-page list of what you own and what you owe. Your organization's board sees the same idea every quarter as a statement of financial position. Buying a home changes that page more than almost any other decision you will make.

On the day you close, cash drops, a large asset appears, and a 30-year loan shows up on the other side. Your net worth does not change on day one, but your liquidity falls sharply. That matters if your position is funded by a grant that ends in 18 months.

The Federal Reserve's [Survey of Consumer Finances](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/scf20.pdf) shows why people buy. In the 2019 survey, median net worth for homeowners was roughly $255,000, against about $6,300 for renters. That gap is real, but part of it reflects who tends to buy: people with steadier income and more savings. It does not prove that any particular house will build wealth for any particular buyer.

So before you compare payments, write down three things:

- Cash you could put toward a purchase, and cash you must keep as an emergency reserve.
- Monthly take-home pay, and how much of it is stable.
- How long you realistically expect to stay in Laramie.

The third item drives the answer more than any of the others.

## Price the full cost of owning, not just the mortgage

The mortgage payment is the number people compare to rent, and it is the smallest part of the story. Here is an illustrative $300,000 home with 10 percent down, a 30-year loan at 6.75 percent, and a comparable rental at $1,500 a month. These are example figures, not a quote for any specific property.

| Monthly cost | Own | Rent |
|---|---|---|
| Principal and interest on $270,000 | $1,750 | n/a |
| Property tax (assumed) | $150 | n/a |
| Homeowner's insurance (assumed) | $125 | n/a |
| Maintenance at 1 percent of value per year | $250 | n/a |
| Rent | n/a | $1,500 |
| **Total** | **$2,275** | **$1,500** |

The gap is about $775 a month. Part of the principal portion of that payment is you paying yourself, because it builds equity. In year one, though, only about $2,900 of the $21,000 in annual payments goes to principal. The rest is interest.

Maintenance is the line people skip. A furnace in a Wyoming winter, a roof after a hailstorm, or a water heater that quits in January all come out of your pocket, not a landlord's.

## Count what the down payment would have earned elsewhere

The down payment and closing costs on that $300,000 home add up to roughly $39,000: $30,000 down plus about 3 percent in closing costs. That money has a job to do whether it sits in a house or somewhere else.

If it stays in a savings account or a conservative portfolio earning 4 percent, it produces about $1,560 in the first year. That is a real cost of buying even though it never shows up on a mortgage statement. If your organization's board has ever sorted reserves into buckets, you already understand the idea. The same discipline applies to household savings, and our post on [keeping a balanced investment portfolio on a schedule](/resources/strategically-balancing-your-investment-portfolio-why-set-it) covers how to think about it.

There is a flip side. If you would not invest the difference and would spend it instead, owning can work as forced savings. Be honest with yourself about which person you are. The math can only reflect the behavior you actually have.

## Run both sides over the years you plan to stay

Now put the pieces together. Using the same example, assume the home appreciates 3 percent a year, rent rises 3 percent a year, and selling costs run about 7 percent of the price.

| Five-year result | Buy | Rent |
|---|---|---|
| Cash paid out (payments, upkeep, upfront costs) | about $175,600 | about $95,600 |
| Net sale proceeds after loan payoff and selling costs | about $70,000 | n/a |
| Growth on the $39,000 kept invested at 4 percent | n/a | about $8,450 |
| **Net cost over five years** | **about $105,600** | **about $87,100** |

Under these assumptions, renting comes out roughly $18,500 ahead after five years. Run the same model at seven and ten years and the gap narrows each year, because the selling costs get spread over more time and more of each payment goes to principal. Change the assumptions and the answer moves. A 5 percent appreciation rate or a 6 percent mortgage rate helps buying. Flat prices or a surprise $12,000 roof helps renting.

That is the point of building it as a model. You are not trying to predict the market. You are finding the break-even year and asking whether you will plausibly still be in the house then.

If you do not have a spreadsheet handy, any rent vs buy calculator will give you a rough answer. Just check what it assumes about maintenance, selling costs, and investment returns, because many leave those out.

## What the mortgage interest deduction does and does not do

Homeowners often count the mortgage interest deduction as a built-in discount. For many households it is smaller than expected. It only helps if your itemized deductions exceed the standard deduction, which for a married couple has been above $29,000 in recent years. A household with a modest mortgage, state tax, and charitable gifts may land under that line and get no extra benefit at all.

IRS [Topic No. 505](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc505) explains which mortgage interest qualifies and the limits on how much debt counts. If you give generously to your own organization or others, your gifts count toward itemizing as well, so run the numbers both ways before you assume the deduction will matter.

It is also worth asking what your return looks like with and without a home. Our [personal income tax team](/personal-income-tax) can run both versions in a few minutes, and that beats guessing.

## Nonprofit paychecks add their own variables

A few details come up often in the Laramie nonprofit world, and they change the math.

**Grant-funded roles.** If your salary depends on a two- or three-year grant, a 30-year loan carries more risk than the same loan for someone with a permanent position. Lenders will look at your income history. You should look at your runway: how many months of housing costs you could cover if the grant did not renew?

**Student loans and forgiveness programs.** If you are on an income-driven repayment plan or working toward public service loan forgiveness, a larger mortgage can change how lenders see your debt-to-income ratio. Check your repayment status before you apply, not after.

**Board service and turnover.** Executive directors and program staff move more often than the 30-year loan assumes. If a board turnover or a new funder could send you to another city within five years, the five-year table above is your table, not the ten-year one.

**Variable income from side work.** Many people in the sector also consult, teach, or freelance. Lenders typically want a two-year history of that income. Keep clean records now and you will have a stronger application later.

## When the organization itself is the one deciding

The same question comes up for the nonprofit. Your organization may be paying rent on an office or program space and wondering whether a building would be better. The framework is identical, with a few extra layers.

A building turns cash reserves into a fixed asset, which can be hard to reverse quickly. A funder may restrict how grant money can be spent on property. The board should model maintenance, insurance, and a capital reserve for the roof and the boiler. It should also check whether any property tax exemption applies to the organization before assuming it does.

Read the board package the way a funder would. Does the statement of financial position still show enough unrestricted cash after the purchase? If not, renting longer may be the more responsible answer. Our [nonprofit accounting work](/industries/nonprofits) already includes board-ready financial statements, so the building question fits naturally into that conversation. For forecasting a decision this size, Megan Hanneman, CGMA, builds the budgets and cash-flow projections that make the trade-offs visible.

## Common Questions

**Is renting better than buying?**

Neither is better in general. Renting tends to win when you expect to stay fewer than five to seven years, your income is uncertain, or your savings would be drained by the down payment. Buying tends to win with a longer horizon and stable income. The break-even year in your own model decides it.

**What is the real cost of buying vs renting a home?**

Owning costs more than the mortgage. Add property tax, insurance, about 1 percent of the home's value per year for maintenance, closing costs near 3 percent, and roughly 7 percent to sell. Then subtract the equity you build. Renting costs the rent plus whatever your down payment earns elsewhere.

**Does the mortgage interest deduction make buying cheaper?**

Only if your itemized deductions exceed the standard deduction. Many households with modest mortgages never cross that line. Check [IRS Topic No. 505](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc505) for what qualifies, then compare your itemized total to the standard deduction before you count on the savings.

## Bring your numbers to a free consultation

If you are weighing a purchase, or your board is weighing a building, we would be glad to build the comparison with you using your real figures instead of rules of thumb. The consultation is free, and you will walk away with a clear break-even year and a sense of the risks. [Contact our Laramie office](/contact) to set up a time.

---


### How to plan for unexpected medical expenses at a Laramie nonprofit
URL: /resources/why-tax-advantaged-planning-is-the-real-defense-against-medi

A nonprofit executive director in Laramie can do everything right. Family health coverage, six months of operating reserves at work, a personal savings account with a respectable balance. Then a surgery, a few weeks of lost work, and a string of specialist visits in Fort Collins or Denver add up to a $12,000 hospital bill, and the savings cushion starts draining fast. The cushion did its job. It just wasn't built to do the whole job.

This post is about the other half of the defense: the tax-advantaged accounts and deductions that make each dollar you spend on medical care cost less. It is written for the people who run and work at nonprofits, because your staff, your board treasurer and you as a leader often face this exact squeeze: modest salaries, high-deductible coverage, and a benefits package the organization has some control over.

## Why a savings cushion is only half the plan

An emergency fund is the right first move. It is also easy to overestimate. The Federal Reserve's [Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/report-economic-well-being-us-households.htm) has consistently found that roughly a third of adults could not cover a $400 emergency expense using cash or its equivalent. A real medical event is many times that, and a high-deductible plan can put the first several thousand dollars squarely on you.

There is a second problem. Savings are after-tax money. To put $4,000 in a savings account, you first earned about $5,700 in gross pay, because federal income tax and Social Security and Medicare tax came out first. Every dollar you spend from that account on a medical bill has already been taxed once.

Tax-advantaged tools change that math. They do not replace an emergency fund, but they make the fund last longer and, in the case of an HSA, keep working after the crisis is over. That is how you avoid medical debt: not by hoping the bill never comes, but by arranging your finances so that when it does, you are paying with discounted dollars.

## How an HSA stretches the same dollar further

A Health Savings Account is the strongest tool of the three, and it has a triple advantage. Contributions are deductible (or pulled from your paycheck before income tax), growth inside the account is untaxed, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free. Nothing else in the tax code does all three.

To contribute, you must be covered by a high-deductible health plan and have no disqualifying coverage. For 2025, the HSA limit is $4,300 for self-only coverage and $8,550 for family coverage, plus an extra $1,000 if you are 55 or older. The IRS adjusts these numbers each year, so confirm the current figures before you set contributions.

Here is what that looks like on a $4,000 medical bill for someone in the 22% federal bracket whose HSA contributions run through the employer's paycheck deduction plan:

| | Paid from checking account | Paid from HSA (paycheck deduction) |
|---|---|---|
| Gross pay needed | about $5,690 | $4,000 |
| Federal income tax (22%) | about $1,250 | $0 |
| Social Security and Medicare (7.65%) | about $435 | $0 |
| Left to pay the bill | $4,000 | $4,000 |

That is roughly $1,690 of pay you did not have to earn to cover the same bill. These are illustrative figures, not a quote for your return, but the pattern holds for most taxpayers. If you fund an HSA on your own rather than through the employer, you still get the income tax deduction. You just miss the Social Security and Medicare savings.

Three details trip people up:

- **The account has to exist first.** Expenses incurred before the HSA is open generally are not qualified, so open it before the surgery is scheduled, not after.
- **The money rolls over.** Unlike a spending account that resets, an unused HSA balance stays yours, even if you change jobs.
- **Records matter.** You can reimburse yourself years later for a qualified expense, but only if you can prove the date and amount. A simple folder of bills and explanation-of-benefits statements is enough.

Wyoming has no state income tax, so for Laramie residents the savings are federal. If you live or work in Colorado or Nebraska, your state return adds another layer we check separately.

## What your nonprofit can do as the employer

Your organization pays no income tax, but your employees do, and the benefits plan is where the nonprofit can help them most. Three decisions sit with the board or the executive director.

**Set up a cafeteria plan.** This is the plan document that lets employees fund HSAs and flexible spending accounts with pre-tax paycheck deductions. Without one, the Social Security and Medicare savings in the table above disappear. The paperwork is modest, and it costs the organization little.

**Consider an employer HSA contribution.** Even $500 a year per eligible employee is tax-free to the employee and is often cheaper for the organization than a raise of the same size, because it avoids employer-side Social Security and Medicare tax on the contribution when made through a cafeteria plan. For a Laramie nonprofit with eight employees, that is a $4,000 line in the budget, and it is a concrete answer when someone asks what the organization does for health costs.

**Put it in the budget before the crisis.** Benefit costs belong in your forecast. Megan Hanneman, CGMA, works with management teams on budgeting and forecasting, and benefit contributions are one of the line items that are easy to model now and painful to improvise later. If a funder requires an audit or a bookkeeper leaves mid-year, a documented benefits plan is one less thing to untangle. Our [nonprofit accounting work](/industries/nonprofits) already covers Form 990 and 990-T filing, board-ready financials and audit preparation, so benefits fit naturally into the same conversation.

One caution: HSA contributions through a cafeteria plan must follow nondiscrimination rules, so they cannot tilt toward highly paid staff. Confirm the design with your CPA before you announce anything.

## Using the medical expense deduction when the bill is large

The itemized medical expense deduction is the safety net for bills the HSA did not cover. It is also the most misunderstood. You can deduct only the portion of unreimbursed medical costs above 7.5% of your adjusted gross income, and only if your total itemized deductions beat the standard deduction.

A worked example: say your AGI is $80,000. The 7.5% floor is $6,000. If you have $18,000 in unreimbursed medical costs that year, $12,000 is deductible. At a 22% bracket, that is about $2,640 back. With $5,000 in costs, you deduct nothing.

That floor is why timing matters. If you know a procedure is coming, you can sometimes bunch elective care, such as dental work, vision, or a planned surgery, into the same calendar year as a bill you cannot avoid, so the total clears the floor. Deferring it to January resets the clock.

The list of what counts is longer than most people think. [IRS Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) covers it, and it includes:

- Insurance premiums you pay with after-tax dollars (not those paid through an employer's pre-tax plan)
- Prescription drugs and insulin
- Mileage to medical appointments at a per-mile rate the IRS sets each year, which adds up when your specialist is 65 miles away in Fort Collins or about 130 miles away in Denver
- Lodging for out-of-town treatment, within limits
- Dental, vision and hearing care

Here is the catch with HSAs: you cannot deduct an expense you paid from the HSA, because it was already tax-free. Keep the two lanes separate on your return.

## Flexible spending accounts reward people who check the deadline

A health flexible spending account also uses pre-tax paycheck dollars. For 2025, the limit is $3,300, and unlike an HSA you do not need a high-deductible plan. The tradeoff is the use-it-or-lose-it rule. Employers may allow a carryover of up to $660 (for 2025) or a grace period of up to two and a half months, but not both, and some offer neither.

Two practical points for nonprofits. First, you generally cannot contribute to a standard health FSA and an HSA in the same year, though a limited-purpose FSA for dental and vision is allowed alongside an HSA. Second, if your organization offers an FSA, put the deadline on the staff calendar in October. Employees forfeit more money at year-end than they realize, and a reminder email costs nothing.

## A simple order of operations

If you are deciding where the next dollar goes, this order works for most households we talk with:

1. Build a starter cushion of one month of expenses so a bill doesn't land on a credit card.
2. If you have an HSA-eligible plan, contribute enough to cover your annual deductible, ideally through paycheck deductions.
3. Add the rest of your emergency fund, targeting three to six months of expenses.
4. Fill the HSA toward its annual limit if cash flow allows.
5. Keep medical records organized so the itemized deduction, if you qualify, takes minutes rather than days.

Organizations can mirror this: [match your insurance coverage to your net assets and cash flow](/resources/insuring-where-it-counts-avoid-over-insuring-in-the-wrong-pl), then put the benefits design in writing.

## Common Questions

**How much should I save for unexpected medical expenses?**

At minimum, save your plan's out-of-pocket maximum, which for 2025 can be as high as $8,300 for self-only and $16,600 for family coverage on an HSA-eligible plan. An HSA lets you build that amount with pre-tax dollars, so it takes less gross pay than a regular savings account.

**Can a nonprofit offer HSAs if it doesn't pay income tax?**

Yes. The organization offers the plan, and the tax benefit goes to employees. A cafeteria plan lets staff fund HSAs through paycheck deductions, and the nonprofit can add its own contribution. Contributions must follow nondiscrimination rules, so confirm the design with a CPA first.

**Is the medical expense deduction worth itemizing for?**

Only when your unreimbursed medical costs exceed 7.5% of AGI and your total itemized deductions beat the standard deduction. With an $80,000 AGI, the first $6,000 is not deductible. Bunching elective care into one year is the most common way to clear the floor.

## Plan before the bill arrives

The best time to set up an HSA, a cafeteria plan or a bunching strategy is before anyone is in a hospital bed. If you run a Laramie nonprofit, or work at one, and want to see how these tools fit your staff, your budget and your return, our locally owned team is glad to walk you through it. As an independent member of the BDO Alliance USA, we bring the resources of a larger network with the responsiveness of a local office, and your first consultation is free. [Contact RML and Associates CPAs](/contact) to get started, or read about how our [advisory team](/advisory) helps clients look ahead so they can plan with confidence.

### Take back control of subscription creep at your Laramie nonprofit
URL: /resources/take-back-control-of-subscription-creep

Most nonprofit budgets get scrutiny on the big lines: salaries, rent, program costs. The $29 here and $75 there rarely get a second look. That is exactly where the leak is. A donor database nobody opened since the last board turnover, a video conferencing plan with six seats and two users, a design tool that renewed for a full year on a card the former office manager used. Each one is small. Together they behave like a recurring expense that was never approved.

Subscription creep is what happens when monthly and annual charges pile up faster than anyone reviews them. For a Laramie nonprofit running on grants, membership dues and a few good fundraisers, it deserves the same discipline as your insurance, your utilities or your payroll-sized commitments: a line in the budget, an owner, and a date when someone looks at it again.

## Why recurring charges deserve a budget line

A one-time purchase goes through a decision. Somebody asks, somebody approves, somebody writes the check. A subscription skips that step after the first month. It renews on its own, quietly, and the charge lands in the ledger under a vague vendor name that nobody connects to a program.

Here is an illustrative example. Say a Laramie nonprofit with a $150,000 annual budget carries these recurring charges:

| Subscription | Monthly | Annual | Question to ask |
|---|---|---|---|
| Donor database | $129 | $1,548 | Are we using the tier we pay for? |
| Email marketing | $75 | $900 | Is the list size still driving the price? |
| Video conferencing (4 licenses) | $64 | $768 | How many people logged in last quarter? |
| Design software | $30 | $360 | Does a free nonprofit plan exist? |
| E-signature | $25 | $300 | How many documents did we send? |
| Cloud storage | $60 | $720 | Do we have two storage accounts? |
| Online giving add-on | $49 | $588 | Is it duplicating a platform feature? |
| Volunteer scheduling app | $40 | $480 | Who still uses this? |
| **Total** | **$472** | **$5,664** | |

That is close to 4 percent of the budget, committed without a single vote. Trim even three of those lines and you free up roughly $1,800 a year for something your mission can actually point to, like a workshop series, a program supply order or a reserve contribution.

## Where subscriptions hide in a nonprofit

Nonprofits have a few habits that make creep worse than it is at a typical business.

**Staff and volunteer turnover.** When a bookkeeper or program coordinator leaves, their logins, saved cards and renewal emails often go with them. Charges keep coming, sometimes to an email address nobody checks. A departing staff member is one of the most common triggers we see for a clean-up, and it is much easier to do on purpose than in a panic.

**Board turnover.** New treasurers inherit a chart of accounts and a pile of vendors with no explanation. Nobody wants to cancel something that might be important, so everything stays.

**Nonprofit pricing that expires.** Many software vendors offer discounted nonprofit plans, but the discount may require annual re-verification. Miss it, and the price jumps to the standard rate without a phone call.

**Free trials that convert.** A volunteer signs up for a fundraising tool for the spring gala. The trial rolls into an annual plan in June. The gala is long over.

**Personal cards and reimbursements.** Subscriptions paid by a board member or staff member and reimbursed later never show up as a recurring pattern in your bank feed. You only see them as scattered reimbursement requests.

**Overlapping tools.** Three people each picked a different tool for the same job. One chose a scheduling app, one a shared calendar add-on, one a project board. All three are still being paid for.

## How to run a subscription audit in one afternoon

You do not need special software. You need twelve months of bank and credit card statements, your general ledger, and someone with the authority to say yes or no. A short, practical sequence works well:

1. **Pull every recurring charge.** Sort twelve months of transactions by vendor name. Anything that appears monthly, quarterly or once a year at the same amount goes on the list.
2. **Add the hidden ones.** Check reimbursement requests, PayPal or other payment processors, and any card held by a staff member, board member or volunteer.
3. **Assign an owner to each line.** A name, not a department. If no one claims it, that is useful information.
4. **Record the renewal date and cancellation terms.** Annual plans often require 30 days' notice. A cancellation that comes one day late costs a full year.
5. **Mark each line keep, downgrade, consolidate or cancel.** Be honest about who actually used the tool in the last 90 days.
6. **Move the survivors into a single schedule** that lists vendor, monthly cost, annual cost, owner, renewal date and the program or grant it supports.

Most boards are surprised by two things. The total is bigger than they guessed, and a handful of lines have no owner at all.

## Grants, restrictions and the Form 990

This is where subscription creep stops being a budgeting annoyance and starts affecting compliance.

If a funder reimburses part of your software costs, the charge generally has to fall inside the grant period and relate to the funded work. A subscription that began under a grant and keeps running after the grant ends should not keep getting coded to that grant. A funder who requires an audit, or simply asks for backup, will notice.

Then there is the Form 990. Nonprofits report expenses by function: program services, management and general, and fundraising. A donor database is mostly fundraising. A scheduling tool for a youth program is program expense. Your accounting software subscription is management and general. When every software charge is coded to "office expense," your functional allocation gets blurry, and that blurriness shows up in the ratios your board and funders look at. If you want a reminder of how these filings work, our [nonprofit accounting page](/industries/nonprofits) covers Form 990 and 990-T preparation and board-ready financial statements.

A clean subscription schedule makes this easier. Each line already carries a function and, where it applies, a grant. Allocation becomes a matter of reading the list instead of reconstructing it in March.

## Set a few rules so it does not creep back

An audit helps for about a year. Rules keep the savings.

- **One approver for new recurring charges.** Anything that auto-renews, including free trials, needs a yes from the executive director or treasurer before a card goes in.
- **A shared organizational email for signups.** Renewal notices go to a mailbox that survives staff changes, such as billing@ at your domain, not a personal inbox.
- **One card for subscriptions.** Put recurring charges on a single organizational card with a modest limit, so the monthly statement is the review tool.
- **Calendar the renewal, not the cancellation.** Set a reminder 45 days before each annual renewal date and decide then.
- **A quarterly five-minute review.** The treasurer reads the subscription schedule at the board meeting. If it takes longer than five minutes, there are too many lines.

Megan Hanneman, CGMA, works with management teams on budgeting, forecasting and cost analysis, and this is the kind of review that fits neatly into that work. It is not a special project. It is a recurring line in the budget that gets a recurring look. And for organizations still running older desktop software next to three or four add-ons, Liz Powers, CPA, can help sort out which tools overlap when you move to a cloud platform. You can read more about our [accounting support](/accounting) if you want help setting up a schedule like this.

## Make the savings count

Cancelling a subscription only helps if the money goes somewhere on purpose. Before the audit, decide where the freed dollars will go. A few ideas that tend to land well with boards:

- Top up an operating reserve, even $150 a month.
- Cover the deductible gap on an insurance policy. If you are wondering whether you are carrying the right amount, our post on [how much insurance coverage a Laramie nonprofit needs](/resources/insuring-where-it-counts-avoid-over-insuring-in-the-wrong-pl) walks through sizing it to net assets and cash flow.
- Fund a specific program line that keeps getting trimmed.
- Move dollars into a designated reserve bucket, which is part of the discipline in our piece on [keeping a balanced investment portfolio on a schedule](/resources/strategically-balancing-your-investment-portfolio-why-set-it).

When you tell the board that the audit freed $1,800 and it now funds a named purpose, the exercise stops feeling like penny-pinching. It becomes a decision.

## Common Questions

**How often should a nonprofit review its subscriptions?**

A full audit once a year is enough for most organizations, with a quick quarterly check by the treasurer. Tie the annual review to budget season, so decisions about cancelling or downgrading flow straight into next year's numbers. Add a review any time a staff member or board officer leaves.

**Are software subscriptions an allowable grant expense?**

Often yes, but only when the grant terms allow it, the cost falls inside the grant period and it supports the funded work. A tool shared across programs usually needs a documented allocation. Check your award agreement, and keep the invoice and your allocation method in the grant file.

**Where do subscriptions go on a nonprofit's Form 990?**

They are reported as expenses in the functional categories: program services, management and general, or fundraising, depending on what the tool supports. A donor database leans toward fundraising, while accounting software sits in management and general. Shared tools may need a reasonable, consistent allocation.

## Talk with a Laramie CPA about your recurring expenses

If your board has never seen a list of every recurring charge, that is a good first conversation. RML and Associates CPAs is locally owned, and we take the time to walk through your statements with you and explain what we find in plain language. Call us or [contact us](/contact) to set up a free consultation, and we will help you build a subscription schedule your treasurer can actually use.

### Lease vs buy a car for a Laramie non-profit: which costs less?
URL: /resources/auto-leasing-vs-buying-which-makes-more-sense

Most advice about leasing versus buying a car assumes you are hoping to write it off. A non-profit is not. If your Laramie organization is tax-exempt, Section 179, bonus depreciation and lease deductions don't lower your tax bill, because there is no tax bill to lower. That one fact flips the usual dealership pitch, and it means the decision comes down to cash flow, grant rules, reporting and how many miles your staff really drive.

Here is the framework we walk board treasurers and executive directors through when a van, a pickup or a staff sedan comes up for replacement.

## Why the usual tax argument flips for a tax-exempt organization

A for-profit owner who buys a work vehicle can often deduct a large share of the cost in year one. [IRS Publication 946](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p946) lays out how Section 179 and depreciation work, including the caps on passenger vehicles. Lease payments, by contrast, are deducted over the lease term, with a small income inclusion for pricier vehicles. Those trade-offs drive a lot of the "buy it before December 31" advice.

None of it helps a 501(c)(3). Your organization doesn't pay federal income tax on income related to its mission, so a deduction has nothing to offset. When a salesperson says "you can write this off," the honest answer is that it doesn't matter to you.

What does matter:

- The total cash that leaves your account over the time you will actually use the vehicle
- Whether a grant or donor restriction allows the purchase
- How the vehicle appears on your balance sheet and your audit
- What happens when your needs change in year three

## When a tax deduction still matters

There are a few narrow cases where the tax side comes back into play.

If the vehicle is used in an unrelated trade or business, such as a thrift shop's delivery van hauling goods for a revenue stream that isn't tied to your mission, that activity can generate unrelated business income reported on Form 990-T. Depreciation or lease costs allocated to that activity can reduce it. You would need clean mileage logs showing how much use is mission-related and how much is not.

Personal use is the other one. If a director takes the organization's car home and uses it for errands, the value of that personal use is generally a taxable fringe benefit and belongs on their W-2. It is easy to miss, and it is one of the cleaner ways a well-meaning organization ends up with an uncomfortable conversation later.

If a donor gives you a vehicle, the rules change again, and we would want to see the paperwork before you sell or keep it.

## A Laramie food pantry van, lease versus buy

Here is an illustration with round numbers, not a quote. Say a Laramie food pantry needs a cargo van that runs routes to Rock River, Centennial and the east side of town. The van costs $42,000.

| | Lease (36 months) | Buy (60-month loan at 7%) |
|---|---|---|
| Cash at signing | $2,500 | $0 |
| Monthly payment | $549 | about $832 |
| Payments over 3 years | $19,764 | $29,952 |
| Loan balance after 36 months | None | about $18,600 |
| Estimated van value after 36 months | Returned to lender | about $27,000 |
| Net cash cost over 3 years | about $22,300 | about $21,500 |
| Mileage cap | 12,000 per year | None |
| Who owns it at the end | The lender | The pantry |

Over three years the two are nearly even, with buying ahead by under $1,000 in this example. The monthly payment is the number that looks cheaper on the lease, and it is the number that misleads people. The lease frees up about $283 a month. Buying leaves the pantry holding an asset worth roughly $8,400 more than the loan balance.

Now change one input. If the van will run 20,000 miles a year, a 12,000-mile lease adds overage charges, often 15 to 25 cents per mile. At 8,000 extra miles a year over three years, that is 24,000 miles, or somewhere between $3,600 and $6,000 in penalties. Buying wins clearly.

Change a different input. If the pantry is rolling out a program that might end when a grant expires in 24 months, a lease with an early termination clause may look worse on paper but be safer in practice. Owning a van you no longer need means selling it, and selling takes time.

## Driving habits in Wyoming that change the math

Miles are where Wyoming organizations get surprised. Laramie is 7,200 feet up, roughly 45 minutes from Cheyenne on I-80 and about 60 minutes from Fort Collins. A program coordinator who drives to a funder meeting in Denver, a site visit in Rawlins and a board dinner in Cheyenne can burn through 12,000 miles in under ten months without noticing.

A few patterns we see:

- **Under 10,000 miles a year, mostly in town.** Leasing can work well, especially if you want a newer vehicle with a warranty and predictable repair costs.
- **15,000 miles or more, or regular highway trips.** Buying usually costs less per mile, since you are not paying for excess mileage or returning a vehicle with wind, gravel and winter wear.
- **Unpredictable use.** If you can't say with confidence what next year looks like, price both options with a higher mileage estimate than you think you need.

Winter matters too. Hail, cracked windshields from gravel on US-287 and the general wear of Wyoming roads all show up at lease return as "excess wear and tear" charges. Read the wear definitions before you sign.

## Is owning a vehicle even the right answer?

Sometimes the cheapest vehicle is the one you don't buy. If staff or volunteers drive a few thousand miles a year for the organization, reimbursing mileage can cost far less than carrying a vehicle, insurance and maintenance. Employees can be reimbursed at the IRS standard mileage rate, which changes annually, so check the current number. Volunteers can be reimbursed tax-free only up to a much lower statutory charitable rate of 14 cents per mile, and anything above that is generally taxable to them. We covered how that plays out in our post on [tax deductions for volunteering](/resources/your-time-is-priceless-but-the-irs-wont-deduct-it-what-you-c).

If the number of miles is high and the use is predictable, a vehicle usually wins. If it is low and scattered, reimbursement usually does.

## Grants, boards and audits shape the answer

This is the part most auto blogs skip, and it is often the deciding factor.

**Grant restrictions.** Many funders limit or require prior approval for equipment purchases, and federal awards have their own thresholds and conditions on titles and disposal. A lease payment may be an allowable operating cost when a purchase is not, or the reverse. Check the award terms before you talk to a dealer, not after.

**Lease accounting.** Under current accounting standards (ASC 842), a non-profit with a lease longer than 12 months generally records a right-of-use asset and a matching liability on its balance sheet. So a lease is no longer "off the books" the way it once was. If your organization is audited or a lender reads your statements, a 36-month vehicle lease will show up.

**Board approval and capitalization policy.** Many organizations have a threshold, such as $5,000, above which purchases are capitalized and need board sign-off. A lease can slip under the radar in a way a purchase cannot, and then a treasurer finds it in the books. Settle who approves vehicle commitments before the paperwork lands.

**Insurance.** Coverage differs for owned, leased and hired vehicles, and lenders on leases often require higher limits. Our post on [sizing insurance coverage for a Laramie non-profit](/resources/insuring-where-it-counts-avoid-over-insuring-in-the-wrong-pl) explains how to match limits to your actual exposure.

## Financing and cash reserves

If you buy, the interest rate matters more than most people expect. The Federal Reserve's [G.19 consumer credit report](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/) publishes average new-car loan rates, which gives you a benchmark for judging the rate a dealer offers. A 1.5 percentage point difference on a $42,000, 60-month loan is roughly $1,700 in interest.

Then ask where the down payment comes from. Paying $8,000 in cash from operating reserves might leave you thin for a month when a grant reimbursement is late. If the organization holds board-designated reserves, our piece on [keeping a balanced investment portfolio on a schedule](/resources/strategically-balancing-your-investment-portfolio-why-set-it) explains how to decide which bucket a vehicle purchase should draw from.

Megan Hanneman, CGMA, works with management teams on cost analysis and budgeting. A vehicle decision is a good place for it: build a five-year cost model with fuel, insurance, maintenance and the replacement cycle, then compare both options on the same basis.

## Questions to settle before you sign

1. How many miles will this vehicle drive each year, with a realistic buffer?
2. Does any grant or restricted gift cover or limit this purchase?
3. Who approves the commitment, and does it fit your capitalization policy?
4. Will any use be unrelated to your mission, or personal?
5. What is the early termination cost if the program ends?
6. Is reimbursing mileage cheaper than owning?

If you can answer those six, the lease versus buy choice usually becomes obvious. If you can't, that is the useful conversation to have before anyone talks monthly payments.

## Common Questions

**Can a non-profit take the Section 179 vehicle deduction?**

Generally no, because a tax-exempt organization has no income tax to reduce on mission-related activity. The deduction can matter only if the vehicle supports an unrelated business activity reported on Form 990-T. Even then, only the business-use share counts, so keep a mileage log.

**Is leasing cheaper than buying for a non-profit?**

Leasing has the lower monthly payment, but over three to five years buying often costs about the same or less, since you keep the vehicle's value. Leasing tends to win with low, predictable mileage and a short program horizon. Buying wins for high mileage or long-term use.

**Does a vehicle lease show up on a non-profit's financial statements?**

Yes, in most cases. Under ASC 842, a lease longer than 12 months is generally recorded as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. Auditors, lenders and funders reading your statements will see it, so include it in your budget and board reporting.

## Talk it through before you sign

A vehicle is one of the larger decisions a Laramie non-profit makes, and the numbers are easier to read with someone who has seen how grants, audits and Form 990 reporting interact. If you are weighing a lease against a purchase, [contact RML and Associates](/contact) for a free consultation. Bring the dealer quotes and your grant terms, and we will walk through them with you until the choice makes sense.
